newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Dresdner shake-up part of global trend.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Dresdner shake-up part of global trend.

text.p: Dresdner Bank's radical restructuring of its fund management business is another sign that financial powerhouses are waking up to the potential of retirement savings, a senior fund manager said on Monday.
"There's a massive move in fund management and it's getting other financial companies interested," said Christopher Day, joint managing director of Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd.
"They will soon start acquiring asset management companies, otherwise they are going to get squeezed. Everybody is trying to become high value-added."

Dresdner said on Friday it was incorporating Thornton & Co, RCM Capital Management and the institutional asset management businesses of Kleinwort Benson Investment Management into a new company lead by RCM.
The unit, whose name and launch date are not yet finalised, will have assets of US$50 billion and spearhead Dresdner's asset management business outside Germany.

"Whether it's central banks -- Dresdner has a lot of central bank business -- or whether it's Mrs Wong in Hong Kong, combined resources is something every client will benefit from in all parts of the company," Day said.

Large financial powerhouses are showing an increasing interest in acquiring fund management subsidiaries, revealing a growing awareness of the power of institutional pension funds, which are now estimated to hold at least US$5 trillion.
Dresdner's move follows Liechtenstein Global Trust AG's recent acquisition of Chancellor Asset Management Inc, boosting assets under management to more than US$80 billion.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell -- itself a merged entity between Deutsche Bank and its own investment banking business, Morgan Grenfell -- said in September it would consider buying a U.S. asset management company to help extend its European position.

Day said an increasing number of wealthy financial services companies are aware that they risk losing business to competitors who have established a stronger position as global fund managers by offering more value for money.

Paine Webber, Goldman Sachs, Merrill Lynch and HSBC Asset Management are all wealthy companies whose competitive edge is being eroded by better-placed firms such as SBC Brinson, formed after Swiss Bank Corp's 1994 acquisition of Chicago-based Brinson Partners.
"They are in the danger zone," he said. "They are smaller, charging the same fees but with fewer resources."

A recent merger between British fund manager Invesco Plc and U.S. mutual fund company AIM Management Group Inc shows that smaller, high value-added fund managers have also become aware of the trend, and are moving to protect themselves, Day added.
The Invesco/AIM merger created one of the world's largest investment management businesses, with about US$150 billion in assets. It will be called AMVESCO Plc.

"Insurance companies might also get involved. They're huge asset managers," Day said. "They could say 'We should do this A large portion of the money comes from the United States, where assets under management among the top 12 U.S. companies grew by an estimated 41 percent in 1995.
"Europe will have to go to private schemes, too, because their public schemes are underfunded," Day said.
